test_title: SSC MTS 2025 Official Paper (Held On: 05 Feb, 2026 Shift 3)
subject: general
question:
In the given question, a sentence is divided into four parts and given in the alternatives (A), (B), (C), and (D). There is an error in one part. Choose the alternative containing that part of the sentence that has the error. Choosing the alternative with the error will be the answer.

It was rude about the professor's daughter to have rejected the red rose which was being given by the young student.

options.text: rejected the red rose which was
being given by the young student.

solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the use of the preposition "**about**" after the adjective "**rude**."
 
• In the grammatical construction "*It is + adjective + [preposition] + person + to-infinitive*," we use "**of**" to indicate that the adjective describes the character or behavior of the person mentioned.
 
• The correct phrase should be "**rude of the**," as the rudeness is an attribute being assigned to the professor's daughter based on her action.
 
• Thus, the error is located in **Option 1** of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"It was **rude of the** professor's daughter to have rejected the red rose which was being given by the young student."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: "professor's daughter to have"** – This part is correct; the possessive form ("professor's") and the start of the perfect infinitive are grammatically sound.
 
• **Option 3: "rejected the red rose which was"** – This part is correct. "Which" is used as a relative pronoun to refer to the rose.
 
• **Option 4: "being given by the young student."** – This uses the passive continuous form ("was being given"), which is appropriate to describe an action that was in progress at that time.
 
• **Common Error:** Many learners mistakenly use "about" or "for," but adjectives like *polite, kind, brave, mean, clever,* and *stupid* always take "**of**" when describing someone's conduct in this specific sentence pattern.
